G:aga-sbs#fluids-ors.text: Instead of large amounts of water, a glucose-electrolyte oral rehydration solution (ORS) is preferred in short bowel syndrome to enhance absorption and reduce secretion, because glucose in the gut stimulates sodium absorption, which water follows.

G:aga-sbs#fluids-sports-drinks.text: Oral rehydration solutions differ from commercial sports drinks: an ORS has considerably more sodium and less sugar.

G:pd-2017#hypotonic-jejunostomy.text: Drinking large quantities of water is a major misconception in short bowel syndrome; patients, particularly those with an end jejunostomy, may benefit from a glucose-electrolyte oral rehydration solution instead.

G:pd-2017#ors-sodium.text: The optimal sodium concentration of an oral rehydration solution in short bowel syndrome is 90 to 120 mmol/L (mEq/L); the clinician decides who needs one from urine output, low blood pressure, recurrent dehydration and kidney injury.

G:pd-2017#simple-sugars.text: In short bowel syndrome, simple sugars and sugar alcohols are limited in both foods and fluids; sodas, fruit juices, fruit drinks and sweet teas are avoided because the sugar in these drinks is related to how much output follows.

draft.verdict: Pantoprazole 40 mg is an acid medicine that guidelines say helps after major bowel surgery, but it comes as a coated, delayed-release tablet, and guidelines warn that this kind of tablet may not be fully absorbed with your parent's end-jejunostomy, so it is worth asking the care team about.

why.claim: Acid medicines like proton pump inhibitors are the main long-term treatment for the extra stomach acid that can follow short bowel surgery.
After a large bowel resection, the stomach can make extra acid for 6 to 12 months. Acid medicines help reduce it. Guidance suggests using them sparingly after 12 months unless they clearly help.
This medicine is a delayed-release tablet.
The label says the tablet has an enteric coating, so the medicine only starts to be absorbed after the tablet leaves the stomach.
All oral proton pump inhibitors have an enteric coating, so they may not be absorbed well in short bowel syndrome.
Guidance on short bowel syndrome says sustained-release and delayed-release medicines should be avoided.
If an oral proton pump inhibitor isn't working early after surgery, guidance says it is reasonable to try one given through a vein (IV).
The label says not to split, crush, or chew the tablets.
The tablet's inactive ingredients include mannitol, which is a sugar alcohol.
Sugar alcohols in medicines can make diarrhea worse in short bowel syndrome.
Of 13 people with an end-jejunostomy (no colon) who logged this medicine, 6 said it helped, 2 noticed no change, and 5 said it caused problems.
Of 8 families with an end-jejunostomy (no colon) who reported what their own care team did, 2 said the form was changed, 1 said monitoring started, 3 said nothing changed, and 2 hadn't decided yet.

evidence.G:aga-sbs#acid-suppression: Massive bowel resection is associated with gastric acid hypersecretion that may last 6 to 12 months; acid-suppressing medicines such as proton pump inhibitors or H2 blockers are beneficial in reducing gastric secretions. It has been suggested they be used sparingly beyond 12 months unless there is clear benefit.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#diet-fat-jejunostomy: People with an end-jejunostomy do not appear to benefit from fat restriction; more fat is absorbed when more is eaten.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#fluids-hypertonic: In short bowel syndrome, hypertonic drinks such as fruit juices and sodas should be limited to reduce output, particularly with net secretion and a high-output jejunostomy.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#fluids-sports-drinks: Oral rehydration solutions differ from commercial sports drinks: an ORS has considerably more sodium and less sugar.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#medications-release-forms: Solid medicines have to disintegrate and dissolve before they can be absorbed, and most oral medicines are absorbed in the proximal jejunum, so many can be used in short bowel syndrome; sustained-release and delayed-release medicines, however, should be avoided.
evidence.G:pd-2017#simple-sugars: In short bowel syndrome, simple sugars and sugar alcohols are limited in both foods and fluids; sodas, fruit juices, fruit drinks and sweet teas are avoided because the sugar in these drinks is related to how much output follows.
evidence.G:pg139#enteric-coating: Delayed-release and enteric-coated tablets have a coating that delays disintegration and dissolution until the tablet has passed through the stomach.
evidence.G:pg139#liquid-forms: For people whose upper gut was resected, liquid forms such as oral solutions or suspensions can improve absorption, but sugar alcohols such as sorbitol and xylitol in them can make diarrhea worse. People with short bowel syndrome rarely have had upper-gut resections.
evidence.G:pg139#ppi: Proton pump inhibitors are the primary medicines used as maintenance therapy for gastric acid hypersecretion in short bowel syndrome. All oral proton pump inhibitors have an enteric coating, so their absorption may be limited in short bowel syndrome; if an oral one is not working early after surgery, a trial of an intravenous one is reasonable.
evidence.G:pg139#sugar-alcohols: Sugar alcohols such as sorbitol and xylitol, found as inactive ingredients in some medicines, can make diarrhea worse in short bowel syndrome.
evidence.G:remane-2025#formulation-classes: In this study, oral formulations were grouped by risk in ostomy patients: noncritical (accelerated release, such as chewable or effervescent tablets, granules and liquids), potentially critical (regular release, such as coated tablets and hard capsules) and critical (modified release, such as enteric-coated, matrix and prolonged-release products).
evidence.G:sood-2013#formulation: When poor absorption is suspected, liquids, capsules and uncoated tablets are likely to be better absorbed, and it may be necessary to avoid modified-release (slow-, controlled- or sustained-release) or enteric-coated formulations.
evidence.G:sood-2013#liquid-excipients: Before using a liquid medicine, its osmolarity, inactive ingredients and volume should be considered: high-osmolarity liquids can cause osmotic diarrhoea, and products containing sorbitol can in theory cause diarrhoea.
evidence.G:sood-2013#ppi: Proton pump inhibitors are often used in people with a short gut to reduce the volume of upper gut secretions.
evidence.G:sood-2013#residual-length: In most cases a stoma is not the main factor in drug absorption; absorption correlates with the length of small intestine remaining, and with a jejunostomy or ileostomy, using medicines normally depends largely on that remaining length.
evidence.G:who-ors#purpose: Oral rehydration solution works because glucose and sodium are absorbed together in the small bowel, carrying water with them.

why.claim: The label lists this medicine as a delayed-release tablet.
The label says the tablets have an enteric coating, so the medicine only starts to absorb after the tablet leaves the stomach.

One guideline says all pantoprazole-type tablets and capsules taken by mouth have an enteric coating, so they may not absorb as well in short bowel syndrome. If one isn't working early after surgery, trying it through a vein (IV) is reasonable.
Another guideline says most medicines absorb in the upper small bowel, but delayed-release and sustained-release forms should be avoided in short bowel syndrome.
A third guideline says that when poor absorption is suspected, it may be necessary to avoid enteric-coated forms. Liquids, capsules and uncoated tablets are likely to absorb better.
The medicine itself has a real job here: after a large bowel surgery the stomach can make too much acid for 6 to 12 months, and acid-lowering medicines like this one help reduce it.
The label says not to split, crush or chew these tablets.
The tablet's inactive ingredients include mannitol, which is a sugar alcohol.
A guideline says sugar alcohols such as sorbitol and xylitol in some medicines can make diarrhea worse in short bowel syndrome.
Other people with an end-jejunostomy logged mixed results: 6 of 13 said it helped and 5 of 13 said it hurt.
Of 8 families with an end-jejunostomy who asked their own care teams about it, 2 had the form changed, 3 had no change, 1 started monitoring and 2 had not decided yet.

evidence.G:pd-2017#simple-sugars: In short bowel syndrome, simple sugars and sugar alcohols are limited in both foods and fluids; sodas, fruit juices, fruit drinks and sweet teas are avoided because the sugar in these drinks is related to how much output follows.
evidence.G:pg139#enteric-coating: Delayed-release and enteric-coated tablets have a coating that delays disintegration and dissolution until the tablet has passed through the stomach.
evidence.G:pg139#liquid-forms: For people whose upper gut was resected, liquid forms such as oral solutions or suspensions can improve absorption, but sugar alcohols such as sorbitol and xylitol in them can make diarrhea worse. People with short bowel syndrome rarely have had upper-gut resections.
evidence.G:pg139#ppi: Proton pump inhibitors are the primary medicines used as maintenance therapy for gastric acid hypersecretion in short bowel syndrome. All oral proton pump inhibitors have an enteric coating, so their absorption may be limited in short bowel syndrome; if an oral one is not working early after surgery, a trial of an intravenous one is reasonable.
evidence.G:pg139#sugar-alcohols: Sugar alcohols such as sorbitol and xylitol, found as inactive ingredients in some medicines, can make diarrhea worse in short bowel syndrome.
evidence.G:remane-2025#formulation-classes: In this study, oral formulations were grouped by risk in ostomy patients: noncritical (accelerated release, such as chewable or effervescent tablets, granules and liquids), potentially critical (regular release, such as coated tablets and hard capsules) and critical (modified release, such as enteric-coated, matrix and prolonged-release products).
evidence.G:sood-2013#formulation: When poor absorption is suspected, liquids, capsules and uncoated tablets are likely to be better absorbed, and it may be necessary to avoid modified-release (slow-, controlled- or sustained-release) or enteric-coated formulations.
evidence.G:sood-2013#liquid-excipients: Before using a liquid medicine, its osmolarity, inactive ingredients and volume should be considered: high-osmolarity liquids can cause osmotic diarrhoea, and products containing sorbitol can in theory cause diarrhoea.
evidence.G:sood-2013#ppi: Proton pump inhibitors are often used in people with a short gut to reduce the volume of upper gut secretions.
evidence.G:who-ors#purpose: Oral rehydration solution works because glucose and sodium are absorbed together in the small bowel, carrying water with them.

swapToAskAbout.text: When poor absorption is suspected, guidelines say liquids, capsules and uncoated tablets are likely to be absorbed better than slow-release forms. This is something to ask the pharmacist or prescriber about. It is not a change to make at home.

draft.verdict: Whether to crush it is a decision for your parent's pharmacist or prescriber; the label says not to crush or chew this tablet, and guidelines raise concerns about extended-release forms for your parent's anatomy.

why.claim: The label says the tablets are scored and can be divided, but they should not be crushed or chewed, whether whole or divided.
This medicine is an extended-release tablet.

Changing a solid medicine's form, for example by crushing it, can change how well it is tolerated or how well it works, so guidelines recommend checking the product information or asking a pharmacist.

After a large part of the bowel has been removed, guidelines say sustained-release or extended-release products should generally be avoided, because how much of the drug gets absorbed can be unpredictable or very poor.
The colon plays only a small part in absorbing medicines, mostly slow-release ones. Your parent has no colon in continuity, so that part of the gut is not there to help.
A colon in continuity can add a lot to how well some drugs are absorbed, and metoprolol is named as an example.
If a medicine is not working in short bowel syndrome, the care team may consider changing its form (for example a crushed tablet, a capsule or a liquid) or how it is given.
Of 9 families with an end-jejunostomy (no colon) who reported what their own care team did about this medicine, 4 said the team changed the form.
Of 9 families with an end-jejunostomy (no colon), 3 said their care team started monitoring.
Of 11 people with an end-jejunostomy (no colon) who logged this medicine, 5 said it went badly for them, 3 said it helped and 3 noticed no difference.

evidence.G:aga-sbs#medications-proximal-absorptio: Most oral medicines are absorbed in the upper small bowel, so many medicines can still be used in short bowel syndrome when they are not sustained- or delayed-release forms.
evidence.G:aga-sbs#medications-release-forms: Solid medicines have to disintegrate and dissolve before they can be absorbed, and most oral medicines are absorbed in the proximal jejunum, so many can be used in short bowel syndrome; sustained-release and delayed-release medicines, however, should be avoided.
evidence.G:hong-2021#absorption-findings: Across 50 studies of 37 drugs in short bowel syndrome, decreased absorption was found for 29 drugs, 6 of which lost their therapeutic effect.
evidence.G:hong-2021#colon-absorption: A colon in continuity can contribute significantly to the absorption of some drugs (for example metoprolol), and drugs absorbed in the colon or over a wide window are least likely to be malabsorbed.
evidence.G:pg139#crushing-immediate-release: If a medicine is not working in short bowel syndrome, the care team may consider changing its formulation (for example a crushed tablet, a capsule or a liquid) or its route.
evidence.G:pg139#extended-release-avoid: After extensive resection, sustained-release or extended-release products should generally be avoided, because the extent of drug absorption can be erratic or severely impaired.
evidence.G:pg139#malabsorption-suspect: In short bowel syndrome, malabsorption of a medicine is an important consideration, particularly when the expected response to it is not seen.
evidence.G:pg139#time-release: Time-release formulations, such as extended-release or controlled-release tablets, are designed to make the drug available for absorption over an extended period, especially in the small intestine.
evidence.G:remane-2025#formulation-classes: In this study, oral formulations were grouped by risk in ostomy patients: noncritical (accelerated release, such as chewable or effervescent tablets, granules and liquids), potentially critical (regular release, such as coated tablets and hard capsules) and critical (modified release, such as enteric-coated, matrix and prolonged-release products).
evidence.G:sood-2013#ask-before-changing-form: If a solid dose form is altered, for example crushed or opened, its tolerability or efficacy can change, so checking the product information or asking a pharmacist is recommended.
evidence.G:sood-2013#colon-slow-release: The large intestine has a minimal role in drug absorption, mainly limited to slow-release drugs and drugs that act in the large intestine.
evidence.G:sood-2013#formulation: When poor absorption is suspected, liquids, capsules and uncoated tablets are likely to be better absorbed, and it may be necessary to avoid modified-release (slow-, controlled- or sustained-release) or enteric-coated formulations.
